method: All 10 supplemental nonempty timed English transcripts read fully, using complete generated readable.txt and recovering truncated portions directly from sentence_timings.json. No video frames/audio inspected. Inventory timestamps below are minutes:seconds from rounded readable transcripts.

video_inventory.evidence: 00:24–00:52 frames explanation as inventing a currency by progressively removing trust. 02:36–03:43 establishes communal ledger and first fraud; 06:37–07:15 discovers replay loophole and adds unique IDs; 10:13–11:37 distributed copies create consensus problem. 12:48–13:34 varies one input character to show hash sensitivity; 16:50–17:21 follows a changed block propagating through linked hashes. 19:43–21:40 tests security by narrating an adversary's attempted fork.
standouts: Requirements arise from failures of the current design; each cryptographic mechanism repairs a newly exposed loophole.
Narration operationalizes actors, messages, and dependencies rather than relying on geometry. A deliberate adversarial simulation earns the trust claim.
video_inventory.exception: A systems-design walkthrough rather than geometric derivation; signature internals are explicitly black-boxed at 05:38–05:49. Historical 2017 parameters and informal security statements must not be treated as current or rigorous guidance.

video_inventory.evidence: 01:14–01:29 explicitly says this is intuition, not a complete proof. 02:02–02:12 adds an asymmetric image to a symmetric square so actions can be tracked. 03:18–03:56 identifies circle actions by a marked point; 06:24–07:50 tracks zero under sliding, 10:11–11:50 tracks one under scaling. 13:57–14:32 plants additive horizontal/vertical versus multiplicative stretch/rotation comparison; 18:23–20:55 repays it with exponentiation. 23:51–24:08 describes rolling the plane into a cylinder then mapping it into concentric circles.
standouts: A visual aid is introduced specifically to make an otherwise invisible operation observable: asymmetric marker on symmetric object.
Changing which anchor is followed (zero vs one) makes addition and multiplication different action systems; remembered structural analogy prepares the later inference.
video_inventory.exception: The narration deliberately supplies a rich interpretation rather than full proof, with optional terse calculus explanation on screen. One transcript example reports a questionable 30-degree angle for 2+i: verify math independently.

video_inventory.evidence: 00:29–01:49 challenges perfect self-similarity as the whole concept. 03:08–07:44 lines/squares/cubes/Sierpinski copies establish how mass scales before fractional dimension is named. 09:14–11:30 exposes limits of that toy model, introduces box counting, and admits the rendered numerical ratio converged surprisingly slowly. 13:27–14:53 asks viewer-as-programmer how to estimate exponent, then derives a log-log slope. 15:38–18:18 distinguishes zoom-dependent effective dimension and pure limiting/applied scale-range meanings.
standouts: A beautiful idealized example is explicitly treated as scaffolding, then replaced because it cannot cover the intended real phenomenon.
Measurement procedure bridges qualitative roughness to a numeric exponent; the plot transformation is justified by the question of how to estimate that exponent.
video_inventory.exception: Empirical and applied explanation with candid animation feedback, not only clean mathematical proof. Fractal definition is qualified, and roughness estimates are contextual historical claims.

video_inventory.evidence: 01:01–01:19 prioritizes how a solution could be discovered over its short final form. 01:51–04:21 reduces sphere/tetrahedron to circle/triangle, fixes two points, varies third, and averages a highlighted arc. 04:26–05:52 shows that route becomes difficult in 3D, then returns to the 2D result's suspiciously clean 1/4. 06:08–07:32 reframes random points as random lines plus coin flips; 07:45–08:32 transfers the resulting finite counting argument to 3D. 08:40–09:11 distinguishes visual understanding from formal write-up.
standouts: Shows a useful method reaching its limit instead of presenting an effortless uninterrupted solution.

Explicit general heuristic: when an added construction helps, try reframing the whole question in terms of it. Lines through the center become the sampled objects, replacing a hard area-average calculation by finite equiprobable choices.
video_inventory.exception: The key change is the generative model for randomness, not a continuously morphed shape; visual proof is explicitly separated from a formal linear-algebra version.

video_inventory.evidence: 03:20–04:23 rejects confusing projected 4D slices in favor of four literal coordinate sliders; 04:38–06:48 calls coordinate squares real estate and uses nonlinear tick spacing to encode cost. 07:05–08:43 fixes one slider and maps remaining motion to familiar slices. 08:44–09:09 says slider play risks being aimless without a problem. 11:48–12:17 rejects shock as the aim, replays familiar dimensions in the new representation. 16:33–22:27 slider budgets explain why an inner hypersphere grows outside a box. 23:25–24:47 honestly states local/coordinate-dependent limits.
standouts: Visual thinking need not mean making a picture that resembles the object; interface-like sliders faithfully externalize analytic constraints.
Repeated reference-frame changes measure the same slider configuration relative to the corner and the origin, making a counterintuitive high-dimensional fact feel causally reasonable.
video_inventory.exception: Strong counterexample to a universal continuous-plane or directly geometric visual template. Representation is intentionally coordinate-bound and local, with stated limitations.

video_inventory.evidence: 00:11–00:40 poses finite usefulness of infinite math but postpones philosophy until a concrete case. 00:44–03:17 motivates a pixel-to-frequency map, then attaches pixels to a woven line and unravels it. 03:58–05:14 recursively builds pseudo-Hilbert curves; 06:06–07:16 follows one frequency as resolution changes to distinguish stable Hilbert from unstable snake mapping. 09:10–14:11 distinguishes every finite approximant from the limit; 14:13–14:51 explicitly lists three unproved obligations. 15:43–17:36 returns to the same stability property underlying practical and infinite contexts.
standouts: A practical design requirement (preserve learned spatial meaning through resolution upgrades) supplies the exact property needed to define the limiting object.
A fixed input is followed through a sequence of functions; this makes convergence a property of outputs rather than an impression of increasingly intricate pictures.
video_inventory.exception: Proof obligations are deliberately enumerated rather than executed. Narration proposes a hypothetical assistive application, not demonstrated product success.

video_inventory.evidence: 01:11–02:34 contrasts a short calculus derivation with the longer goal of locating the hidden circle and previews the whole dependency chain. 02:35–05:45 counts lattice points via rings and reveals apparent irregularity; 05:48–08:25 reinterprets sum of squares as complex conjugate product. 12:54–17:49 physically organizes conjugate factors into two columns and varies placements, linking counted choices back to points on circles. 18:39–18:54 names this as the hardest step and invites paper. 26:07–27:54 parks factor four in a corner, reorganizes rows into columns, then brings it back for the final sum.
standouts: Visual algebra is literal bookkeeping: column placements are possible factorizations, output products are lattice points, and a parked factor remains a remembered obligation.
Long-form narrative repeatedly re-states the original counting purpose during abstract detours so the audience knows why each tool is being introduced.
video_inventory.exception: Almost half-hour, technically dense layered exposition; key Gaussian-prime theorem is taken as given at 11:39–11:58. Not evidence that every explanation should be short or derive all prerequisites.

video_inventory.evidence: 00:19–01:38 explicitly chooses foundational wave mathematics over isolated quantum surprise. 01:46–02:30 defines physical meaning of field arrows; 04:26–06:22 changes view toward screen, suppresses magnetic field, follows one electric vector and introduces cosine parameters/kets. 06:23–08:09 adds oscillations tip-to-tail and varies phase to explain elliptical/circular polarization. 08:18–09:46 picks a basis to match the filter. 13:26–15:17 lets classical energy-splitting fail for indivisible photons, then an experiment motivates probability reinterpretation; 18:25–20:25 compares retained mathematics with changed interpretation.
standouts: Layered selective attention—whole field to one vector to components—reduces visual load without losing what the arrows mean.
Reuses one mathematical representation while explicitly changing its interpretation at the classical/quantum boundary; the old intuition is stressed by a concrete experimental prediction.
video_inventory.exception: A science model-building collaboration with historical/physical assertions and omitted derivations. Transcript alone is not validation of the quantum explanation or a complete physics account.

video_inventory.evidence: 02:06–03:22 reframes integer triangles as lattice points at integer distances, then proposes complex squaring. 03:23–05:30 combines algebraic preservation of integer coordinates with geometric squaring of length in several examples. 06:55–08:15 animates all z to z² using colored grid lines to preserve identity and exposes organized arcs. 08:24–10:18 openly identifies missed triples and adds radial-line multiples. 10:22–14:20 moves to rational unit-circle points and an angle correspondence to establish completeness; 11:33–11:46 discloses finite displayed sample.
standouts: Separate guarantees are made visible: integer output coordinates follow algebra, integer length follows geometry. Neither alone proves the target property.
The elegant generating picture is not allowed to stand as an all-solutions proof; explicit missing examples trigger a second representation and completeness argument.
video_inventory.exception: Two different proof jobs—construction and exhaustion—require different pictures. Transcript has duplicated text and reversed interval around 14:00–13:59; exact pacing there unreliable.

video_inventory.evidence: 00:03–04:30 foregrounds other educators' actual attempts/failure on mugs before theory. 06:08–06:21 promises to rediscover the formula from the puzzle, not introduce it unexplained. 06:22–08:27 reframes focus to regions, lights a starting vertex, and lets each added edge either light a vertex or close a region. 09:25–11:06 counts edge/region incidences to prove planar impossibility; 11:10–12:09 generalizes to Euler's formula only afterward. 12:21–15:57 returns to handle-based successes; 16:38–17:08 withholds answer to exactly where the plane proof fails on a mug.
standouts: Illuminated/unilluminated state is a counting invariant: the animation's visible state changes directly encode the algebraic conservation law.
Real failed attempts precede an impossibility proof, and the end challenge asks viewers to debug the proof's precise assumption rather than repeat a topological slogan.
video_inventory.exception: Social montage and physical puzzle participation, with unusually long delayed entry into narrated theory. Caption corruption around 09:13–09:18 means local timing/content needs care.

additional_generalizations: Useful additions to a picture often become the new objects of the problem: point-pairs, lines through center, enclosed regions, factor columns. Hardest-problem and three-utilities state this as a transferable problem-solving heuristic.

Working through a method's failure is part of explanation: 3D arc averaging becomes hard; complex squaring misses triples; self-similarity fails to define ordinary disks; ledger signatures leave replay attacks. New machinery arrives as a repair with an explicit job.

Visual fidelity means fidelity to mathematical constraints, not necessarily resemblance to physical geometry: higher-dimensional sliders, actor/message diagrams, and factor-column bookkeeping all satisfy the deeper style pattern.

Exceptional formats matter: narrated derivation, pedagogical manifesto, numerical exploration, interview, participant montage, and systems design all occur. Do not reduce the style to one narrative template or solely dark-background geometry.
